Every card eventually fails. Usually the higher-quality cards have better error correction mechanisms, are manufactured more precisely and last longer. One of the most important things you can do is to be careful when writes are occurring. Don't pull out a card when it's still being written on.

This is how flash drives work, not sure if SD cards use the same method. Each flash/USB/thumb drive is divided into tiny sections. On a hard drive platter it's called a "cluster". So a 64-bit OS can track more clusters on a hard drive than a 32-bit OS because the 64-bit OS supports larger numbers. (It was a really big deal for some advanced users of Windows when Windows went to 32-bit because, at the time, Windows was not keeping up with larger hard drives.)

Each section on a thumb drive can be written to about 1000 times. If a section wears out, the drive controller (on the drive itself) is supposed to mark that section bad, and move your data in that section somewhere else. After years of writes, you will eventually see the available space start to decrease. But for cheaper flash drives, some electronics tend to fail first because they are cheap components.
